cards.back: At equilibrium in a simple binding model, the ligand concentration associated with half occupancy.
A change in one binding event's effect on the affinity of additional sites in a multisite system.
Turnover number: catalytic cycles per enzyme molecule per unit time at substrate saturation.
Inhibition that raises apparent Km in the simple model while preserving Vmax at saturating substrate.
An electrochemical proton gradient across a membrane that can power transport and ATP synthesis.
A molecule such as NAD⁺/NADH that transfers electrons between metabolic reactions.
The rate at which material flows through a reaction or pathway.
Use of labeled atoms to follow molecular transformations and estimate pathway flow.
v = Vmax[S]/(Km + [S]); Km is the [S] at half Vmax and is not generally a dissociation constant.
kcat = Vmax/[E]₀ (needs active enzyme); kcat/Km is the low-substrate second-order rate constant.
Competitive: Km×α, Vmax same. Noncompetitive: Vmax/α, Km same. Uncompetitive: both ÷α.
Prefer nonlinear fits over double-reciprocal fits; spread [S] around Km and keep rates initial.
ΔG = ΔG°′ + RT ln Q; direction depends on ΔG, not ΔG°′. RT ≈ 2.58 kJ/mol at 310 K.
Cells hold ATP/ADP far from equilibrium, so cellular ΔG for ATP hydrolysis is more negative than −30.5 kJ/mol.
Standard free energies add when reactions share a mechanism, as in hexokinase's phosphoryl transfer.
ΔG°′ = −nFΔE°′; NADH to O₂ releases about −219 kJ/mol, stored stepwise as a proton gradient.
K_d = [R][L]/[RL]; θ = L_free/(K_d + L_free); half occupied at L_free = K_d.
Use the quadratic when receptor is not ≪ K_d; otherwise binding is overestimated.
Y = Pⁿ/(P₅₀ⁿ + Pⁿ); n > 1 positive cooperativity; n ≤ number of sites.
A sigmoidal curve unloads far more between lung and tissue pressures than a hyperbola.
Base: f(BH⁺) = 1/(1 + 10^(pH − pKa)). Acid: f(A⁻) = 1/(1 + 10^(pKa − pH)). Half at pH = pKa.
pI = average of the two pKa values bracketing the neutral form; neutral amino acids use the α-carboxyl and α-amino pKa values.
Net charge falls as pH rises; above the pI it is negative (moves toward the positive electrode, binds anion exchange).
A group buffers within about one unit of its pKa; histidine (pKa about 6) is the main protein buffer near neutral pH.
K_u = [U]/[N] = exp(−ΔG_unfold/RT); f_N = 1/(1 + K_u); RT = 2.48 kJ/mol at 25 °C.
ΔG_unfold([D]) = ΔG_H₂O − m[D]; midpoint C_m = ΔG_H₂O/m.
ΔΔG of −8 kJ/mol multiplies K_u by about 25; the folded fraction may barely change while the unfolded supply rises sharply.
Stabilities of a few tens of kJ/mol leave a small unfolded population that chaperones and degradation systems must manage.
Glucose → 2 pyruvate with a net 2 ATP and 2 NADH; lactate fermentation reoxidizes the NADH, giving 2 lactate per glucose.
[AMP] ≈ K[ADP]²/[ATP] with K ≈ 1; EC = ([ATP] + ½[ADP])/([ATP] + [ADP] + [AMP]); a 10% fall in ATP can raise AMP several-fold.
Inhibited by ATP and citrate; activated by AMP, ADP and fructose-2,6-bisphosphate; sigmoidal in fructose-6-phosphate.
A pool can rise from more production or less consumption; crossover patterns locate a block; flux needs rate measurements.
Δp = Δψ + 61.5 mV × ΔpH at 37 °C; the free energy per mole of protons is F × Δp, about 19 kJ/mol for Δp near 196 mV.
Minimum ≈ ΔG_ATP/(F Δp) ≈ 2.7; measured about 4 including transport; efficiency about 68% in the synthetic example.
4 substrate-level + 10 NADH × 2.5 + 2 FADH₂ × 1.5 = 32 (30 to 32 depending on shuttles); 5.3 ATP per O₂.
Proton return without ATP synthesis lowers ATP per O₂, raises oxygen use and heat, and does not block glycolysis.
J = k₁S in a two-step pathway; A_ss = J/k₂; the same pool can follow more production or less consumption.
C_i = (ΔJ/J)/(ΔE_i/E_i); ΣC_i = 1; a linear prediction holds for small changes only.
Control is shared and condition-dependent; the lowest-activity or most-regulated step need not control flux.
Allosteric: seconds. Covalent: seconds to minutes. Enzyme amount: hours to days (time to 90% = ln 10 × half-life / ln 2).
Average the replicate initial rates at each substrate concentration; report the number of replicates.
1/v = (Km/Vmax)(1/[S]) + 1/Vmax: intercept = 1/Vmax, slope = Km/Vmax; unweighted fits magnify error at low rates.
Vmax unchanged, Km(app) = Km(1 + [I]/K_I); K_I = [I]/(α − 1) with α = Km(app)/Km.
Less than about 10% substrate used, negligible product inhibition, concentrations spread around Km.
No NADH reoxidation at the chain → NADH rises → lactate dehydrogenase makes lactate to regenerate NAD⁺ → lactate is a redox outlet.
Glycolysis to lactate gives 2 ATP per glucose; keeping the same ATP with a blocked chain needs glucose uptake of demand/2 and lactate of two per glucose.
Lactate/pyruvate tracks cytosolic NADH/NAD⁺ at equilibrium; an M+3 lactate fraction divided by the labeled fraction of glucose gives the fraction from medium glucose.
Oxygen consumption, lactate/pyruvate, a glucose tracer and an electron-acceptor rescue; use at least two independent readouts.
At pH above its pI a protein is usually net negative and may bind a positively charged anion exchanger; below pI it is usually net positive and may bind a cation exchanger.
Within the fractionation range, larger hydrodynamic particles enter fewer pores and elute before smaller particles.
Total enzyme activity in U divided by total protein in mg gives U/mg; rising specific activity suggests enrichment under comparable assays, not proof of homogeneity.

Total protein = volume × concentration; total activity = volume × activity concentration; recovery = current activity/start activity × 100; fold enrichment = current specific activity/start specific activity.
Per acetyl-CoA: 2 CO₂, 3 NADH, 1 FADH₂, 1 GTP; four-carbon oxaloacetate is regenerated.
Before the cycle, one pyruvate becomes acetyl-CoA, releasing one CO₂ and making one NADH.
Anaplerotic reactions replenish cycle intermediates withdrawn for biosynthesis; pyruvate carboxylase can refill oxaloacetate in many mammalian tissues.
A stable intermediate pool does not prove unchanged flux; production and consumption can change together.
Pyruvate carboxylase uses ATP to make oxaloacetate; PEPCK uses GTP to make PEP.

cards.front: Gluconeogenesis input per glucose from pyruvate
cards.back: 4 ATP, 2 GTP and 2 NADH are consumed. Keep the nucleotide and redox ledgers distinct.
F2,6BP activates PFK-1 and inhibits FBPase-1, favoring glycolysis at this opposing pair.
Glycerol can supply triose phosphate; even-chain fatty-acid acetyl-CoA cannot support net glucose synthesis in mammals.
From free glucose, glycogen incorporation costs 1 ATP to phosphorylate glucose and 1 ATP equivalent to regenerate the UTP used for UDP-glucose.
Glycogen phosphorylase releases glucose 1-phosphate from alpha-1,4 chains; debranching activity releases a small amount of free glucose at alpha-1,6 links.
Liver glycogen supports blood glucose; skeletal muscle glycogen primarily supplies glucose 6-phosphate for local use.
Phosphorylation favors glycogen breakdown by activating phosphorylase and shifting glycogen synthase toward its less-active form.
Per glucose 6-phosphate: 2 NADPH, 1 CO2 and 1 ribulose 5-phosphate; no direct ATP is made.
NADPH supplies reducing power for biosynthesis and redox maintenance; NADH commonly feeds respiratory ATP production.
Three C5 pentose phosphates can rearrange to two C6 fructose 6-phosphates plus one C3 glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate.
G6PD consumes NADP+. NADP+ availability and NADPH feedback inform oxidative-branch flux alongside substrate and network state.
Turns = n/2 − 1; acetyl-CoA = n/2. C16 palmitoyl-CoA yields 7 turns and 8 acetyl-CoA.
Each mitochondrial turn generally yields one NADH and one FADH2; separate these from TCA outputs.
Activation to acyl-CoA costs 2 ATP equivalents; the carnitine shuttle carries long-chain acyl groups into the matrix.
State P/O ratios, TCA outputs, GTP treatment and activation cost before reporting a net ATP estimate.
One nitrogen comes from ammonium through carbamoyl phosphate; the other comes from aspartate. Bicarbonate supplies the carbon.
One urea costs 3 ATP molecules but 4 high-energy phosphate equivalents because one ATP is cleaved to AMP.
CPS1 and OTC are mitochondrial; citrulline moves to cytosol for the remaining reactions.
Argininosuccinate cleavage releases fumarate; malate/OAA and transamination can return carbon to aspartate.
Transamination transfers amino nitrogen; the remaining carbon skeleton enters a separate metabolic route.
Pyruvate and several TCA intermediates can support net glucose synthesis through gluconeogenesis.
Leucine and lysine yield only ketogenic carbon products in the standard classification.
Acetyl-CoA oxidation does not provide net glucose carbon in mammals, despite label exchange across TCA turns.
The commonly grouped ketone bodies are acetoacetate, D-beta-hydroxybutyrate and acetone.
Hepatic mitochondrial beta-hydroxybutyrate/acetoacetate balance responds to the NADH/NAD+ state.
Extrahepatic SCOT activates acetoacetate; thiolase then yields two acetyl-CoA molecules.
Liver synthesizes and exports ketone bodies but lacks SCOT for canonical ketolysis.
One acetyl-CoA primes fatty-acid synthase and seven more become malonyl-CoA: eight acetyl-CoA total per palmitate.
Acetyl-CoA carboxylase uses ATP, bicarbonate and biotin to form malonyl-CoA.
One palmitate synthesis consumes 7 ATP at ACC and 14 NADPH at fatty-acid synthase, excluding acetyl-CoA supply costs.
Malonyl-CoA supplies fatty-acid synthase and inhibits CPT1-mediated long-chain acyl-group entry to mitochondria.
ER membrane HMGCR reduces HMG-CoA to mevalonate using NADPH; it is a major regulated step in sterol synthesis.
Low ER cholesterol permits SREBP2 processing, increasing expression of HMGCR and LDL receptor.
ApoB-48 marks intestinal chylomicrons; ApoC-II activates LPL; ApoE supports remnant uptake; ApoB-100 binds LDLR on LDL.
LPL removes triacylglycerol from liver-derived VLDL through IDL toward cholesterol-rich LDL; LDLR recognizes ApoB-100.
PRPP is activated ribose made from ribose 5-phosphate; it supports de novo purine synthesis, purine salvage and late pyrimidine-ring attachment.
Purines are assembled on PRPP to IMP; pyrimidine rings form first, then orotate receives PRPP to form OMP and UMP.
IMP-to-AMP uses GTP; IMP-to-GMP uses ATP at the branch conversion steps.
Ribonucleotide reductase converts NDP to dNDP; thymidylate synthase uses methylene-THF to convert dUMP to dTMP.
Glycerol-3-phosphate is acylated through lysophosphatidic acid, phosphatidic acid and diacylglycerol; DGAT adds the third acyl chain to form TAG.
Complete hydrolysis of 1 mol TAG releases 3 mol fatty acids and 1 mol glycerol.
ATGL converts TAG to DAG; HSL converts DAG to MAG; MGL converts MAG to glycerol, releasing one fatty acid at each step.
Capillary LPL acts on circulating chylomicron/VLDL TAG; ATGL, HSL and MGL mobilize stored intracellular TAG.
Total measured activity divided by total protein mass; it can support enrichment but does not alone prove purity.
Fraction total activity divided by starting total activity, multiplied by 100%; it is distinct from protein-mass recovery.
Sequential methods that use different properties, such as charge and hydrodynamic size, can add distinct evidence; neither guarantees resolution.
Total protein = volume × protein concentration; total activity = volume × activity concentration.
M+n fractions report isotope labeling; flux (amount per time) requires a defined tracer model, time course and stated assumptions.
With stated P/O values, two acetyl-CoA yield 6 NADH, 2 FADH2 and 2 GTP; SCOT bypasses one GTP-forming step. D-BHB oxidation adds one NADH.
Hepatocytes generally lack SCOT-dependent oxidative ketolysis; a mouse study reported a separate SCOT-independent anabolic route for ketone-derived lipid carbon.

cards.front: What does amino-acid tracer labeling in a biosynthetic pool establish?
cards.back: It can support a substrate contribution in the stated model and pool; it does not by itself establish net glucose production, total flux or whole-body human contribution.

cards.front: What does a mass isotopomer fraction show?
cards.back: M+1/M+2 report molecules with one/two heavy-carbon increments. Label incorporation is not a flux rate; quantify flux with a fitted atom-mapping model and supporting measurements.

cards.front: How does urea-cycle energy cost scale?
cards.back: Per mol urea: 3 mol ATP molecules but 4 mol high-energy phosphate equivalents. Scale from paired nitrogen atoms only under the stated stoichiometric boundary; this is demand, not flux.

cards.front: How do you balance a defined hepatocyte cholesterol pool?
cards.back: Change = synthesis + uptake − conversion − export. Keep this intracellular pool separate from circulating LDL concentration and whole-body balance.
Count PRPP separately for de novo IMP and purine salvage. Then count GTP for IMP-to-AMP and ATP for IMP-to-GMP; these are distinct pathway ledgers.
Net ATP-pool change equals synthesis minus utilization. A zero net change can coexist with substantial synthesis and consumption; a rate is not a concentration or pathway-flux estimate.

cards.front: Three ATP molecules, four phosphate equivalents
cards.back: Per urea, two ATP go to ADP at CPS1 and one ATP goes to AMP plus pyrophosphate at argininosuccinate synthetase, spending two bonds.

cards.front: Average of ratios or ratio of averages?
cards.back: Normalize each culture by its own cell count, then average cultures; dividing the mean amount by the mean cell count weights cultures differently.

cards.front: Label in glucose from a ketogenic amino acid
cards.back: Exchange through citric-acid-cycle intermediates can carry label into glucose without supplying net glucose carbon.

cards.front: Almost fully folded, yet very different
cards.back: A 9 kJ/mol stability loss raises the unfolded population about 38-fold even when both proteins are over 99.9% folded.

cards.front: When is total ligand a safe stand-in for free ligand?
cards.back: When receptor is far below K_d, so bound ligand is a negligible part of the total; otherwise use the quadratic.
Compute recovery and fold enrichment within each run, then average runs; specific activity is not a purity measurement.

cards.front: Is this rate an initial rate?
cards.back: Only if product rises linearly over the window and under about 10% of substrate is consumed; later windows include depletion and product effects.
kcat/Km decides which substrate wins at low, competing concentrations; kcat sets the rate for one substrate at saturation.

cards.front: Which inhibition washes out at high substrate?
cards.back: Competitive inhibition; uncompetitive and noncompetitive inhibition persist because the inhibitor acts on the enzyme–substrate complex.

cards.front: Fit the hyperbola, not its reciprocal
cards.back: Nonlinear least squares on measured rates keeps residuals on their own scale; a reciprocal plot gives the noisiest low rates the most leverage.
Reciprocal fits of noisy data can show a Vmax difference that a nonlinear fit does not, and turn a competitive pattern into an apparent mixed one.
For simple competitive inhibition α = Km(apparent)/Km and K_I = [I]/(α − 1); report the fitting method with the value.

cards.front: When does a near-equilibrium step reverse?
cards.back: When the product/substrate ratio rises above K′eq, making the actual ΔG positive.
Its electrons enter at ubiquinone, after complex I; succinate to ubiquinone releases only about 3 kJ/mol.
A rising M+n fraction shows tracer reaching a pool; flux needs precursor enrichment, pool sizes and a model.

cards.front: Energy charge and the ATP/ADP ratio
cards.back: With adenylate kinase at equilibrium (K = 1), energy charge depends only on ATP/ADP; AMP rises with the square of ADP.
Intermediates before a slowed step rise and those after it fall; the crossing localizes the step but does not measure the flux.

cards.front: Glucose from lactate: the NADH ledger
cards.back: Lactate oxidation to pyruvate makes the NADH that gluconeogenesis consumes, so the redox ledger differs from the pyruvate start.

cards.front: Why fats give less ATP per oxygen
cards.back: More of their electrons enter as FADH₂, which yields 1.5 rather than 2.5 ATP per pair in the course convention.

cards.front: Leak changes ATP per oxygen, not electron flow
cards.back: With 20% proton leak, 32 ATP per glucose falls to 26.4 while oxygen use can stay the same or rise.
Lower ER sterol activates SREBP2, raising LDLR expression and uptake; the cellular ledger is not a plasma LDL balance.
Flux control coefficients sum to 1; a linear estimate holds only for small changes because control shifts as enzymes change.
Fatty-acid synthase uses 14 NADPH per palmitate; the oxidative pentose phosphate branch gives 2 NADPH per glucose 6-phosphate.

cards.front: The decisive measurement for a respiratory block
cards.back: Oxygen consumption: a chain block must lower it, while a primary glycolytic defect need not and would lower lactate.

cards.front: Only active enzyme counts in Vmax
cards.back: Vmax = kcat × [active enzyme]; unfolded or inactive molecules add protein but no rate.
If enzyme and a tight-binding inhibitor are comparable in concentration, binding depletes free inhibitor; use the mass-balance solution.

cards.front: Specific activity as a purity bound
cards.back: Comparing a pool's specific activity with the value expected from kcat and molar mass bounds the active-enzyme fraction, if no contaminant contributes activity.

cards.front: Glucose to fat, but not fat to glucose
cards.back: Pyruvate dehydrogenase is effectively one-way and acetyl-CoA gives no net oxaloacetate, so even-chain fat carbon cannot become net glucose.
An uncoupler raises oxygen use while ATP falls; a chain inhibitor collapses oxygen use and pushes NADH into lactate.
Nonoxidative transketolase and transaldolase reactions can rearrange glycolytic intermediates into pentose phosphates when ribose demand exceeds NADPH demand.

cards.front: Only folded protein binds in the staged model
cards.back: Compute R_F = f_folded × R_T first, then use R_F, not R_T, in the ligand-depletion quadratic.
[RL]/R_F is the bound fraction of folded protein; [RL]/R_T is the fraction of all protein that is folded and bound.
In the project model, net charge informs solubility and resin choice but does not determine folding stability or K_d.

cards.front: What distinguishes flux from thermodynamic drive?
cards.back: A rate also depends on mechanism,occupancy and turnover;the driving ratio alone does not determine it.

cards.front: What must accompany a membrane-potential sign?
cards.back: The transfer direction and inside-minus-outside potential convention,with each transported charge and chemical term explicit.

cards.front: How is an integer transport bound verified?
cards.back: Check the candidate and next integer against the signed complete-cycle inequality under the same gradients and energy boundary.

cards.front: What evidence distinguishes a transport mechanism?
cards.back: Compatible signed fluxes,concentrations,coupling and perturbations that address competing pathways,not one endpoint alone.

cards.front: Why are ATP molecules and phosphate equivalents different?
cards.back: ATP-toAMP charging consumes one ATP molecule but is assigned two equivalents under the stated regeneration ledger.

cards.front: What belongs in a translation energy result?
cards.back: Residue count,charging convention,elongation boundary,overhead and retry/quality-control assumptions.

cards.front: Which denominator defines an output error fraction?
cards.back: All accepted outputs under the declared selection boundary,including both correct and incorrect survivors.

cards.front: What does a two-filter probability model leave unresolved?
cards.back: Real kinetic steps,energy costs,correlations and substrate-specific pathways need their own evidence.

cards.front: Why distinguish net triose output from regenerated intermediates?
cards.back: Counting retained cycle carbon as exported product would violate the net carbon and energy boundary.

cards.front: What must be specified with a light-reaction yield?
cards.back: Electron sources/sinks,productive excitation boundary,proton-route assumptions and omitted losses.

cards.front: Why can enough reductant still leave an energy deficit?
cards.back: ATP and NADPH demands are distinct constraints,and their supply ratio depends on the declared coupling and electron pathways.

cards.front: What makes a carbon-output maximum defensible?
cards.back: It satisfies every carbon,energy and reductant constraint under one declared boundary.

cards.front: How can two cycles have equal free energy but different transport?
cards.back: Their species counts,gradients and permitted kinetic paths can differ even when the signed sums agree.

cards.front: Why retain separate ledgers inside one report?
cards.back: Each model’s counts,selection denominator and omitted costs must be auditable before any cross-model interpretation.

cards.front: What must a resource-limited synthesis preserve?
cards.back: The limiting amount,all stoichiometric inputs and remaining resources,with cycle intermediates separated from net output.

cards.front: Why can identical final photon counts conceal different mechanisms?
cards.back: Different proton-coupling and cyclic-route assumptions can yield the same aggregate;intermediate species and energy ledgers identify the actual model.

P = v/(a₀ l_c). Below about 1/3: spherical micelles; 1/3–1/2: cylindrical micelles; 1/2–1: bilayers; above 1: inverted phases. Two chains roughly double v, which is why phospholipids make bilayers and single-chain detergents make micelles.

T_m rises with saturated chain length and falls sharply with cis double bonds. Cholesterol orders a fluid bilayer and prevents crystallization below T_m; at high content it gives a liquid-ordered state.

Integral proteins need a detergent to release, peripheral ones come off with salt or pH, lipid-anchored ones hold a covalent lipid. A transmembrane α-helix needs about 20 nonpolar residues: 3 nm ÷ 0.15 nm per residue.

In the plane ⟨r²⟩ = 4Dt. FRAP mobile fraction M_f = (F_∞ − F₀)/(F_i − F₀). Flip-flop takes hours unaided; with equal rates, asymmetry decays as e^(−2kt), halving in half the single-molecule flip half-time.
θ = [L]/([L] + K_d). With efficacy τ, R = (1 + τ)θ/(1 + τθ) and EC₅₀ = K_d/(1 + τ). Spare receptors put EC₅₀ below K_d; removing receptors shifts EC₅₀ before lowering the maximum.
Active receptor = GEF: Gα swaps GDP for GTP. Gα·GTP stays active for 1/k_hyd on average; RGS proteins (GAPs) shorten it. Output per activation = effector rate × lifetime.

[cAMP]_ss = V_syn/k_PDE, reached with time constant 1/k_PDE. PKA (R₂C₂) needs four cAMP to free two catalytic subunits. PDE inhibition raises cAMP and slows its decay; cholera toxin blocks Gαs GTPase.

Gq → PLCβ: PIP₂ → soluble IP₃ (ER Ca²⁺ release) + membrane DAG (PKC). Insulin receptor → IRS → PI3K → PIP₃ → Akt; PTEN reverses. Steroid receptors bind DNA and act over hours; ligand-gated channels act in milliseconds.
